notes.title: Chapter map: Kubernetes networking
notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection

This section is the network Kubernetes builds on top of the VPC. Kubernetes asks for one property: every pod gets an IP, and every pod reaches every other pod without NAT. Everything else is layered on, and each layer has one surprise:

  • Services balance connections, not requests.
  • DNS tries every search domain before the name you typed.
  • Policies are allow-only and enforced only if the CNI does it.
  • Termination races the propagation of endpoint changes.

Most production incidents in this section come from a default that was fine for HTTP/1.1 and short requests.

Concept map

The flat network comes first because every later note adds a name, a filter or a balancer on top of pod IPs.

Green holds a CORE note, blue is SUPPORTING; 137–138 holds one of each (137 CORE). There are no BREADTH items, so there's no breadth.md. Neighbours: CIDR planning below this section, where pod addresses come from; gRPC load balancing and service mesh beside 139 and 141; inference load balancing after 146.

Reading order:networking modelCNI pluginsServices and kube-proxyheadless ServicesCoreDNSnetwork policiesingress, gateway, meshprobesrolloutsinference LB

CoreDNS and policies are read before the gateway (142 and 143 before 141) because default-deny egress first breaks DNS, and the gateway note assumes both.

Owners

Each idea is explained in full in one note. Other notes link to it and don't repeat it.

How should callers reach this workload? Ask in this order. The first "yes" decides.

notes.title: The Kubernetes Networking Model — Every Pod an IP, No NAT Between Pods
notes.html:
References

Kubernetes: Cluster networking · Kubernetes: Services, load balancing and networking · AWS EKS best practices: VPC CNI · AWS EKS: Assign more IP addresses with prefixes

TL;DR

Kubernetes asks for one thing from the network: every pod gets its own IP, and every pod can reach every other pod without NAT, so the address a pod sees for itself is the address everyone else sees. How that happens is left to the CNI plugin, as an overlay or as real VPC addresses. Three consequences follow. The network is flat and unfiltered by default. Pod IPs are ephemeral, so nothing may depend on one. And on VPC-native clusters every pod spends a real subnet address.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:pod scheduledCNI creates its network namespaceassigns an IP from the node's rangeprograms routesany pod reaches it directly, source IP intactpod dies, IP returns to the pool

Recall

Prompt Answer
The model in one sentence? Every pod has its own IP; pods reach each other directly with no NAT.
How many containers share a pod's IP? All of them: one network namespace, so localhost between containers.
Is a pod IP stable? No. It lives as long as the pod; Services exist because of that.
What does the model leave unspecified? The implementation. The CNI plugin decides overlay vs VPC-native.
Is pod-to-pod traffic filtered by default? No. Any pod reaches any pod until a NetworkPolicy, enforced by the CNI, says otherwise.
Draw by hand: two nodes, three pods node boxes with their IPs; pods inside with their own IPs; arrows pod → pod across nodes labelled "src preserved"; two containers in one pod joined by localhost.

The idea

A team migrates a service from VMs to Kubernetes and keeps its IP allow-list for the payments database, written with node IPs. On VMs that worked: the app's source address was the VM. In the cluster, half the requests fail. On their VPC-native CNI, the database sees each pod's own address, which matches no node on the list and changes on every deploy.

Nothing is broken; the model did what it promises. The source address is the pod, and the pod is temporary.

The trade: a flat, NAT-free network makes pods look like hosts to every tool and protocol, and you pay with addresses that change on every restart, no isolation until you add policy, and (VPC-native) a real address spent per pod.

How it works

Two nodes, three pods; the node is a router, never a NAT.

Rule What actually happens
IP per pod the pod's network namespace gets one IP; every container in it shares that IP and the port space
No NAT between pods pod C sees pod A's IP as the source; NAT happens only at Services and the cluster edge
Node agents reach their pods kubelet probes and daemons talk to pod IPs on the same node directly
Implementation is pluggable the CNI plugin builds the namespace, assigns the IP and programs routes or tunnels
No isolation by default reachability is total; NetworkPolicy, enforced by the CNI, is the only filter 
VPC-native address demand per AZ = (nodes + nodes × pods per node) / AZs   ← 200 × 30 over 3 AZs: 2,067
usable in a /20 = 4,096 − 5 = 4,091 · in a /24 = 251                        ← AWS reserves 5 per subnet
max pods, m5.large, secondary IPs = ENIs × (IPs per ENI − 1) + 2 = 3 × 9 + 2 = 29

Evolution

Lineage:Jun 2014 Kubernetes launches with IP-per-pod2016 CNI becomes the plugin contract2019 VPC-native CNIs mainstream (AWS VPC CNI, GKE alias IPs)Jul 2021 prefix delegation on EKSApr 2025 native sidecars stable (1.33)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the model hasn't changed since 2014.
  • Changed recently: dual-stack IPv4/IPv6 is stable, and IPv6-only EKS clusters sidestep exhaustion entirely.
  • What won't change: the self-view rule; tools from flow logs to mTLS depend on it.

On the wire

What these commands show on any cluster (illustrative addresses, not a captured run), with the default that bites:

kubectl get pods -o wide            # NAME   IP            NODE
                                    # app-a  10.20.18.7    node-1
                                    # app-c  10.20.19.3    node-2
kubectl exec app-a -- hostname -i   # 10.20.18.7   ← the pod's own view = everyone's view
kubectl exec app-c -- sh -c 'nc -l -p 8080 & sleep 1; ss -tn'
kubectl exec app-a -- nc 10.20.19.3 8080
                                    # ESTAB 10.20.19.3:8080  10.20.18.7:51544
                                    # ← source is the pod, not node-1's 10.20.16.5
# the default that bites: no NetworkPolicy exists, so this works from every pod in every namespace

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): how many addresses a VPC-native cluster spends per AZ.

per_az = ceil((200 + 200 * 30) / 3)                    # secondary-IP mode
per_node_prefix = (ceil(30 / 16) + 1) * 16             # whole /28s + 1 warm prefix
print(per_az, ceil((200 + 200 * per_node_prefix) / 3), usable(24), usable(20))
# look for: both against the /24 and the /20
# naive belief predicts: prefix delegation saves addresses

Run: 2,067 per AZ in secondary-IP mode and 3,267 with prefixes, against 251 in a /24 and 4,091 in a /20. Prefix delegation raises pods per node (29 → 434 on an m5.large) but spends addresses in blocks of 16, and it needs free contiguous /28s.

Measure it

  • See it: kubectl get pods -o wide for pod and node IPs; kubectl exec <pod> -- ss -tn on the receiver shows the caller's pod IP as source.
  • In production: free IPs per pod subnet (AvailableIpAddressCount), pods stuck in ContainerCreating with "failed to assign an IP", and the CNI's own IP-pool metrics.
  • Bounded by: address space → CNI choice and a 100.64/10 secondary CIDR; reachability → network policies.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Kubernetes requires a flat network: every pod gets its own IP, any pod reaches any pod directly, and no NAT happens between them, so a pod's own address is the one others see. The CNI plugin implements it, as an overlay or as VPC addresses. So the network is open by default, pod IPs are temporary, and on VPC-native clusters address planning decides how big the cluster can grow.

Q · Mechanism — Why IP-per-pod instead of Docker-style port mapping? Port mapping makes every app negotiate host ports, and the address a service advertises isn't the one it binds. IP-per-pod makes a pod look like a VM: it binds its normal port, DNS and service discovery hand out one real address, and no app needs to know it's containerised. The cost is moved to the network, which now has to route a lot of short-lived addresses.

Q · Trade-off — Overlay or VPC-native pod IPs? VPC-native: pods are real VPC addresses, so load balancers target pods directly, flow logs show pods, and there's no encapsulation, but every pod spends a subnet address. Overlay: a private pod range costs no VPC space, but packets carry a tunnel header and outside systems only see node IPs. VPC-native when external systems must address pods and the CIDR is planned; overlay when address space is scarce.

Q · Failure — New pods stay in ContainerCreating in one AZ only. What happened? That AZ's pod subnet ran out of addresses; others still have room, so it looks like a scheduling bug. With prefix delegation it can also be fragmentation: free addresses exist but no contiguous /28. Fix: a secondary 100.64.0.0/10 CIDR with new pod subnets (custom networking), and alerts on free IPs per subnet.

Q · Design — Cluster networking for a multi-tenant AI platform with GPU inference pods.

  • Addresses: VPC-native CNI with pods in a 100.64/10 secondary range, one /18 per AZ, prefix delegation on.
  • Isolation: a namespace per tenant with default-deny NetworkPolicy, and a policy-enforcing CNI (Cilium or VPC CNI's policy agent).
  • Inbound: Gateway API with an inference-aware route to the model pools, not a plain Service (inference LB).
  • Watch first: free IPs per AZ, cross-AZ bytes, and policy drops.

Compare

VPC-native (AWS VPC CNI, GKE alias IPs, Azure CNI) Overlay (Flannel VXLAN, Calico IPIP, Cilium tunnel)
Pod IP source the VPC subnet: routable a cluster-only range
Reachable from outside the cluster yes, directly only through a Service or gateway
Address exhaustion risk high none in practice
Per-packet overhead none a tunnel header; smaller effective MTU
What flow logs show pod IPs node IPs and tunnel traffic

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
IPs per pod 1, shared by its containers one network namespace spec (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes cluster networking
Max pods, m5.large 29, or 434 with prefixes EKS caps at 110 below 30 vCPUs derived; default (as of Nov 2026): EKS max-pods guidance
Model: 200 nodes × 30 pods, 3 AZs 2,067 per AZ; 3,267 with prefixes /24 = 251, /20 = 4,091 derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Prefix size /28 per slot 16 addresses spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS EKS prefix docs

Pitfalls

  • "A pod IP is like a VM IP: allow-list it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's routable and shows up in logs like any host.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's reassigned on every reschedule, so the allow-list is wrong after the next deploy.
    ↳ Think instead: address Services, identities or CIDR ranges, never a single pod IP.
  • "The cluster network is private, so it's isolated"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: nothing outside can reach it directly.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: inside, every pod reaches every pod in every namespace; one compromised pod sees the whole cluster.
    ↳ Think instead: default-deny NetworkPolicy per namespace from day one.
  • Don't put VPC-native pods in the node subnets.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the default and it works for the first few hundred pods.
    ↳ What goes wrong: pods drain the subnet and new nodes can't even get an address.
    ↳ Do instead: dedicated pod subnets from a 100.64/10 secondary CIDR.
  • "Prefix delegation saves addresses"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the documented fix for running out of pods per node.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it raises pods per node but allocates in blocks of 16 plus a warm block, so a cluster can spend more addresses.
    ↳ Think instead: density per node vs addresses per AZ are separate budgets.
  • Not the same: pod IP vs Service IP
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are cluster IPs that you can curl.
    ↳ Difference: a pod IP is a real interface that lives with the pod; a Service IP is virtual, never on any interface, and stable.
    ↳ Think instead: pods are endpoints, Services are names (Services).
  • Shelf life: the model is durable; CNI modes, max-pods rules and prefix behaviour move.

Connections

Path:CIDR planningthe K8s networking modelCNI pluginsServices
  • Builds on routing basics: a node routes for its pods.
  • Owned elsewhere: the VPC owns subnets and reserved addresses.
  • Breaks when combined with IP allow-lists outside the cluster that assume stable sources.
  • Bounded by network policies: the only filter in a flat network.

notes.title: CNI Plugins — VPC-Native vs Overlay, and Who Enforces Policy
notes.html:
References

CNI specification · Kubernetes: Network plugins · AWS EKS: Amazon VPC CNI · Cilium: kube-proxy replacement

TL;DR

A CNI plugin is the code the container runtime calls when a pod starts and stops. It creates the pod's interface, assigns an IP and programs routes, then undoes all of it on delete. Plugins split on one axis:

  • VPC-native (AWS VPC CNI, GKE, Azure CNI): pods hold real subnet addresses. They're routable from outside but spend your CIDR.
  • Overlay or routed cluster range (Flannel, Calico, Cilium): pods hold cluster-only addresses. They cost no VPC space but are hidden behind node IPs.

Whether NetworkPolicy works at all is the plugin's choice too.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:kubelet asks the runtime for a pod sandboxruntime calls the CNI ADDveth or ENI into the pod netnsIPAM hands out an addressroutes or tunnel entries programmedDEL on teardown returns it

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a CNI plugin do on ADD? Attach an interface in the pod netns, assign an IP, program routes.
Which popular plugin enforces no NetworkPolicy? Flannel: connectivity only; policies are accepted and ignored.
Why do overlays shrink the MTU? The tunnel header (VXLAN: 50 bytes) eats into every packet.

The idea

A team writes careful default-deny NetworkPolicies, applies them, and kubectl reports them created. A penetration test still reaches the database from a random pod. The cluster runs Flannel, which implements connectivity and nothing else, so the API server stored the policies and no component enforced them.

The trade: the CNI plugin decides your address budget, your per-packet overhead and whether policy is real, and you pay for a wrong pick with a migration that touches every pod.

How it works

AWS VPC CNI Cilium Calico Flannel
Pod IP source VPC subnet cluster range, or VPC-native mode cluster range, BGP-routed or tunnelled cluster range
Between nodes native VPC routing tunnel or native routing BGP, IPIP or VXLAN VXLAN
NetworkPolicy yes, via the network policy agent yes, identity-based, L3–L7 yes no
Replaces kube-proxy no yes (eBPF) in eBPF mode no
Address exhaustion risk high low low low

The contract is small: a JSON config in /etc/cni/net.d/, binaries in /opt/cni/bin/, and ADD, DEL, CHECK verbs. Plugins chain: VPC CNI for addresses plus Cilium for policy is a common pairing.

Evolution

Lineage:2015 CNI spec from CoreOS2016 Kubernetes adopts CNI2019 AWS VPC CNI as EKS defaultJul 2021 EKS prefix delegationAug 2023 VPC CNI enforces NetworkPolicy
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: eBPF dataplanes (Cilium, Calico eBPF) replace kube-proxy and the iptables layer; the kube-proxy IPVS mode is deprecated since 1.35.
  • What won't change: VPC-native means addresses spent per pod; overlay means a header per packet.

On the wire

The AWS VPC CNI's settings, with the defaults that bite:

# kubectl -n kube-system set env daemonset aws-node …
ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION: "true"   # default false: one secondary IP per pod caps an m5.large at 29 pods
WARM_PREFIX_TARGET: "1"            # default 1 when prefixes are on: a spare /28 per node, 16 addresses idle
AWS_VPC_K8S_CNI_CUSTOM_NETWORK_CFG: "true"   # default false: pods land in the NODE subnets;
                                   # true + an ENIConfig per AZ puts them in 100.64/10 pod subnets
ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY: "true"      # EKS add-on setting; default false, so policies are ignored

Measure it

  • See it: ls /etc/cni/net.d/ on a node names the plugin; ip -d link in a pod shows veth vs vxlan; kubectl get networkpolicy -A next to an actual blocked nc proves enforcement.
  • In production: IPAM free addresses per node and subnet; pods stuck in ContainerCreating; for overlays, fragmentation or MSS issues after an MTU change.
  • Bounded by: address space (VPC-native) → CIDR planning; policy → network policies.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The CNI plugin implements the pod network: on pod start it attaches an interface, assigns an IP and programs routes. VPC-native plugins give pods real subnet addresses, which are routable but spend CIDR; overlays use a cluster range with a tunnel header. Policy enforcement and kube-proxy replacement are plugin features too, so I pick for addresses and policy together.

Q · Mechanism — What happens between "pod scheduled" and "pod has an IP"? The kubelet asks the container runtime for a sandbox. The runtime creates a network namespace and calls each configured CNI plugin with ADD. The plugin creates a veth pair (or attaches an ENI slot), asks its IPAM for an address, sets routes inside and outside the namespace, and returns the result. If IPAM is empty, the pod waits in ContainerCreating.

Q · Trade-off — Cilium or the AWS VPC CNI on EKS? VPC CNI keeps pods as VPC addresses that load balancers and security groups understand, and AWS supports it. Cilium adds identity-based L7 policy, eBPF instead of iptables, and Hubble flow visibility. Many teams chain them: VPC CNI for addresses, Cilium for policy and observability.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
VXLAN overhead 50 bytes 1,500 MTU → 1,450 inside the tunnel spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 7348
Max pods, m5.large 29; 110 with prefixes (EKS cap) 3 ENIs × 10 IPs default (as of Nov 2026): EKS max-pods guidance
Prefix size /28, 16 addresses per ENI slot spec (as of Nov 2026): AWS EKS prefix docs

Pitfalls

  • "Writing a NetworkPolicy means it's enforced"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the API server accepts it and kubectl get lists it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: enforcement is the CNI's job; Flannel, or VPC CNI without the policy agent, ignores it silently.
    ↳ Think instead: test a blocked connection after every policy change.
  • Don't change the CNI on a live cluster in place.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's one DaemonSet swap.
    ↳ What goes wrong: existing pods keep old interfaces and addresses; mixed nodes can't reach each other.
    ↳ Do instead: new node group or new cluster, then migrate workloads.
  • Not the same: overlay vs VPC-native "Cilium"
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the same plugin name covers both modes.
    ↳ Difference: tunnel mode hides pods behind node IPs; ENI or native-routing mode gives pods VPC addresses.
    ↳ Think instead: name the mode, not just the plugin.
  • "Overlay overhead is negligible"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: 50 bytes is small against 1,500.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a mismatched MTU black-holes large packets, which looks like random hangs on big responses.
    ↳ Think instead: set pod MTU = link MTU − tunnel header, and test with large payloads.
  • Shelf life: the ADD/DEL contract is durable; plugin features, defaults and the kube-proxy story move.

Connections

Path:the networking modelCNI pluginsServices and kube-proxynetwork policies
  • Builds on MTU and fragmentation: the overlay's header tax.
  • Owned elsewhere: CIDR planning owns pod subnets.
  • Breaks when combined with policies on a CNI that doesn't enforce them.
  • Bounded by the bill: VPC-native pods cross AZs like any host.

notes.title: Services & kube-proxy — A Virtual IP That Balances Connections, Not Requests
notes.html:
References

Kubernetes: Service · Kubernetes: Virtual IPs and service proxies · Kubernetes blog: NFTables mode for kube-proxy · Kubernetes blog: Scheduling the removal of the IPVS backend

TL;DR

A Service gives a set of short-lived pods one stable name and one virtual IP. Nothing listens on that IP. kube-proxy (or an eBPF CNI) programs rules on every node that DNAT a new connection to one ready pod, and conntrack pins the connection there. So balancing is L4 and per connection. HTTP/1.1 pools hide this. HTTP/2 and gRPC expose it: five long-lived connections over forty pods leave 88% of them idle, with no error anywhere.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:client resolves orders.shop.svcClusterIP 10.96.10.5node rules matchpick a ready endpoint from EndpointSlicesDNAT to 10.20.18.22:8080conntrack pins every later packet

Recall

Prompt Answer
Does anything listen on a ClusterIP? No. It exists only as dataplane rules on every node.
Balancing unit? The connection: one decision at the first packet, pinned by conntrack.
The three kube-proxy backends in 2026? iptables (default), nftables (GA 1.33, recommended), IPVS (deprecated 1.35).
What does externalTrafficPolicy: Local buy? The real client IP and no second hop; costs even distribution.
ExternalName Service? A DNS CNAME: no ClusterIP, no proxying.
Draw by hand: a ClusterIP connection client pod → node rules (DNAT, conntrack) → one backend pod; label "one decision per connection"; a second request on the same connection follows the same arrow.

The idea

A team scales its gRPC inference service from 8 to 40 GPU pods because latency is climbing. Latency doesn't move. All 40 pods are Ready, no errors anywhere, and 35 of them serve nothing. The 5 gateway pods each hold one HTTP/2 connection to the ClusterIP, and kube-proxy made exactly 5 decisions, once, when those connections opened. Every request since then has ridden one of those 5 connections.

The trade: a Service makes ephemeral pods addressable with zero moving parts in the data path, and you pay with balancing that only happens when a connection opens, so long-lived, multiplexed connections defeat it silently.

How it works

One connection through a ClusterIP: nothing is proxied, the kernel rewrites the address.

Service type Creates Reachable from Use it for
ClusterIP virtual IP + DNS name inside the cluster internal HTTP/1.1 APIs
NodePort a port on every node, plus ClusterIP anything that reaches a node the substrate for LoadBalancer
LoadBalancer a cloud LB, plus NodePort VPC or internet external exposure
Headless (clusterIP: None) DNS returns every pod IP inside the cluster gRPC, StatefulSets, client-side LB (headless)
ExternalName a CNAME inside the cluster aliasing an external dependency 
idle share with c connections over n pods ≈ (1 − 1/n)^c
c = n = 40 → 36% idle · c = 5, n = 40 → 88% idle · c = 400 → ~0%

Evolution

Lineage:2014 userspace proxy2016 iptables mode default2018 IPVS mode GA2020 EndpointSlicesApr 2025 nftables mode GA (1.33)Dec 2025 IPVS deprecated (1.35)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone (stable 1.35) keeps calls in-zone; ServiceCIDR objects (GA 1.33) let you add Service ranges to a live cluster; SIG Network has scheduled IPVS removal.
  • What won't change: a ClusterIP balances connections, whichever backend programs it.

On the wire

Three Services, with the defaults that bite:

kind: Service                      # internal HTTP/1.1: ClusterIP is right
metadata: { name: orders }
spec:
  selector: { app: orders }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone  # default: any zone; 2/3 of calls cross AZs in a 3-AZ cluster

kind: Service                      # gRPC / inference: headless, so the CLIENT balances per request
metadata: { name: inference }
spec:
  clusterIP: None                  # no virtual IP, kube-proxy not involved
  selector: { app: inference }

kind: Service                      # external, keeping the client IP
metadata: { name: edge }
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local     # default Cluster: second hop SNATs the client IP to a node IP

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): per-connection balancing as balls into bins.

def idle(c, n, trials=2000):
    return sum(n - len({randrange(n) for _ in range(c)}) for _ in range(trials)) / trials / n
for c, n in ((40, 40), (5, 40), (400, 40)): print(c, n, f"{idle(c, n):.1%}")
# look for: the 5-connection row
# naive belief predicts: 40 replicas share load evenly once they're Ready

Run: 40 connections over 40 pods left 36.1% idle, 5 left 88.1%, and 400 left 0.0%, matching (1 − 1/n)^c. HTTP/1.1 pools sit in the last row; HTTP/2 sits in the middle one.

Measure it

  • See it: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders lists eligible pods; conntrack -L -d 10.96.10.5 on a node shows each connection's chosen pod.
  • In production: max-to-median requests per pod for every HTTP/2 or gRPC Service; kube-proxy sync_proxy_rules_duration_seconds p99 (rule lag during rollouts).
  • Bounded by: per-connection balancing → headless Services or an L7 proxy (gRPC load balancing); rule programming at thousands of Services → nftables or eBPF.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A Service puts a stable name and virtual IP in front of ephemeral pods. Nothing listens on it: kube-proxy programs rules on every node that DNAT each new connection to one ready pod, and conntrack pins it. So it's L4, per connection: fine for HTTP/1.1 pools, wrong for gRPC and HTTP/2, which need headless Services or an L7 proxy. LoadBalancer and NodePort just add entry points in front.

Q · Mechanism — Where does a ClusterIP connection actually get balanced? On the client's own node, in the kernel. The EndpointSlice controller lists ready pods; kube-proxy watches them and writes iptables or nftables rules; the first packet of a connection matches, picks an endpoint and is DNATed; conntrack reverses it for replies and pins the flow. kube-proxy isn't in the packet path, so killing it breaks nothing until endpoints change.

Q · Trade-off — externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster or Local? Cluster lets any node forward to any pod, so load is even, but the second hop SNATs the client IP to the node's. Local forwards only to pods on the receiving node: no extra hop, the real client IP survives, and nodes without a pod fail the LB health check. Load then follows pod placement. Use Local with even placement (a DaemonSet or topology spread).

Q · Failure — 40 GPU pods, all Ready, 35 idle, no errors. Why? The callers hold a few long-lived HTTP/2 connections to a ClusterIP, and each connection was balanced once. Nothing fails, so no alert fires; only per-pod request counts show it. Fix: a headless Service with client-side round-robin per request, or a gateway or mesh that balances requests, and for inference a queue-aware picker (inference LB).

Q · Design — Service layout for a platform with HTTP APIs, gRPC services and an inference fleet.

  • HTTP/1.1 APIs: ClusterIP with trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone.
  • gRPC: headless Services plus client-side LB, or mesh sidecars or ztunnel waypoints balancing per request.
  • Inference: Gateway API with an InferencePool, never a bare ClusterIP.
  • Edge: one LoadBalancer for the gateway with Local and IP targets; nothing else exposed.
  • Dataplane: nftables mode (or eBPF) before the Service count reaches thousands.

Compare

Backend Lookup Updates Status (Nov 2026)
iptables linear rule chains bulk rewrite, cost grows with the cluster default
nftables maps, near O(1) incremental GA 1.33; recommended on kernel 5.13+
IPVS hash tables incremental deprecated 1.35; removal scheduled
eBPF (Cilium, Calico) BPF maps incremental replaces kube-proxy entirely

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Listeners on a ClusterIP 0 rules only spec (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes virtual IPs
NodePort range 30000–32767 default default (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes Service docs
Idle pods, 5 connections over 40 88.1% (1 − 1/40)^5 derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Idle pods, 40 over 40 36.1% approaches 1/e derived; model run 24 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "A Service is a load balancer running in the cluster"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it has an IP, a port and a balancing story.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: there's no process; rules on every node rewrite addresses in the kernel, once per connection.
    ↳ Think instead: rules, not a box: nothing to scale, nothing to inspect but conntrack.
  • "More replicas behind a ClusterIP means more throughput"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it works for HTTP/1.1 services.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: HTTP/2 and gRPC multiplex onto few connections, so new pods get no connections.
    ↳ Think instead: balance requests with headless Services or an L7 proxy.
  • Don't rely on the client IP with the default traffic policy.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the LB passes it in and logs used to show it.
    ↳ What goes wrong: Cluster SNATs to a node IP, so rate limits and audits key on nodes.
    ↳ Do instead: externalTrafficPolicy: Local with even pod spread, or PROXY protocol.
  • Not the same: ClusterIP vs headless Service
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: same YAML kind, one field apart.
    ↳ Difference: ClusterIP returns one virtual IP and the kernel balances connections; headless returns every pod IP and the client balances.
    ↳ Think instead: who makes the choice: the node or the client.
  • "kube-proxy proxies traffic"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the name says so, and the 2014 userspace mode did.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: in iptables and nftables modes it only programs kernel rules; packets never touch it.
    ↳ Think instead: a controller, not a proxy: if it dies, only updates stop.
  • Shelf life: per-connection balancing is durable; backend defaults, IPVS removal and trafficDistribution values move.

Connections

Path:the networking modelServices and kube-proxyheadless Servicesingress, gateway, mesh
  • Builds on L4 load balancing and NAT: a ClusterIP is DNAT plus conntrack.
  • Owned elsewhere: gRPC load balancing owns the multiplexing problem; the bill owns cross-AZ cost.
  • Breaks when combined with long-lived HTTP/2, gRPC or WebSocket connections.
  • Bounded by rollouts: endpoint lag sends traffic to terminating pods.

notes.title: Headless Services & StatefulSet DNS — No Virtual IP, the Client Chooses
notes.html:
References

Kubernetes: Headless Services · Kubernetes: DNS for Services and Pods · Kubernetes: StatefulSets, stable network ID · gRPC: Load balancing

TL;DR

clusterIP: None removes the virtual IP and kube-proxy from the path. DNS for the Service name then returns every ready pod's IP, and the client decides where each request goes. Two uses follow:

  • Client-side balancing for gRPC and HTTP/2, where a ClusterIP would pin each connection to one pod.
  • Stable identity for StatefulSets: db-0.db.shop.svc.cluster.local names one pod across restarts, even though its IP changes.

Nothing balances for you any more: that's the point and the risk.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:client resolves inference.ml.svcCoreDNS returns 40 A recordsclient opens a connection per podbalances each request across themre-resolves when pods change

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does clusterIP: None remove? The virtual IP and all kube-proxy rules; DNS returns pod IPs instead.
A StatefulSet pod's DNS name? <pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, such as db-0.db.shop.svc.cluster.local.
Who balances now? The client, or the gateway in front: per request if it's built to.

The idea

A Kafka-style cluster runs as a StatefulSet. Broker 2 must tell clients "partition 7 lives on me", and they must reach exactly broker 2, not "some broker". A ClusterIP would send them anywhere. A headless Service gives each pod a DNS name tied to its ordinal (kafka-2.kafka), which survives a restart even though the IP behind it changes.

The same mechanism fixes gRPC. If DNS hands back all pods, the client can hold a connection to each and spread requests, which a ClusterIP's single connection never can.

The trade: removing the virtual IP gives the client per-pod identity and per-request choice, and you pay with balancing, retries and re-resolution becoming the client's problem, and with DNS caching deciding how fast it notices change.

How it works

ClusterIP Service Headless Service
DNS answer for svc one virtual IP one A record per ready pod
Per-pod names none <pod>.<svc> when pods set subdomain (StatefulSets do)
Balancing node rules, per connection the client, per request if it chooses
Not-ready pods removed from rules removed from DNS unless publishNotReadyAddresses: true
Change visible after rule sync (seconds) DNS TTL (CoreDNS default 30 s) plus client re-resolution

StatefulSet pods start in order (db-0 before db-1) by default, keep their names and PVCs across reschedules, and peers find each other through the headless Service named in serviceName.

Evolution

Lineage:2015 headless Services2016 PetSet2017 StatefulSet GA (1.9)2020 gRPC xDS client-side balancing2024 Gateway API GRPCRoute GA
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: proxyless gRPC (xDS) and meshes take over the per-request job that client code used to do from raw DNS.
  • What won't change: a headless Service is a DNS answer and nothing more.

On the wire

A headless Service for a StatefulSet and what DNS returns, with the defaults that bite:

kind: Service
metadata: { name: db, namespace: shop }
spec:
  clusterIP: None                  # no VIP; A records per ready pod
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true   # default false: a starting peer can't be found by the others,
                                   # so a cluster that needs peers to bootstrap never forms
  selector: { app: db }

dig +short db.shop.svc.cluster.local        # 10.20.18.4  10.20.19.7  10.20.17.2   ← every pod
dig +short db-0.db.shop.svc.cluster.local   # 10.20.18.4                            ← exactly one
# illustrative addresses. The default that bites in clients: many resolve once at start-up
# and never again, so pods added later get no traffic until the client restarts

Measure it

  • See it: dig against the Service name (all pods) and a per-pod name (one); kubectl get endpointslices shows what DNS will return.
  • In production: requests per pod (spread), client re-resolution count, and time from a new pod Ready to its first request.
  • Bounded by: client behaviour → gRPC load balancing; DNS freshness → CoreDNS.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A headless Service sets clusterIP: None, so there's no virtual IP and no kube-proxy: DNS returns every ready pod's IP. StatefulSets use it for stable per-pod names like db-0.db, so peers address each other by identity. gRPC clients use it to open a connection per pod and balance requests. The cost is that the client now owns balancing and must re-resolve.

Q · Mechanism — How does db-0.db.shop.svc.cluster.local stay stable when the pod's IP changes? The StatefulSet gives each pod a fixed name and sets its subdomain to the headless Service. CoreDNS builds the per-pod record from EndpointSlices, which carry the pod's hostname. When db-0 is rescheduled it gets a new IP but the same name, and the record updates; clients that cache the old IP past the TTL still break.

Q · Trade-off — Headless Service with client-side LB, or a ClusterIP behind a mesh? Headless puts balancing in each client: no extra hop, but every language needs a correct LB policy and re-resolution. A mesh or proxyless xDS keeps balancing out of app code and adds outlier detection and retries, at the cost of a control plane. Headless for a few gRPC services owned by one team; a mesh when many teams and languages call each other.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
CoreDNS record TTL 30 s kubernetes plugin default ttl default (as of Nov 2026): CoreDNS kubernetes plugin
Records per headless answer one per ready pod large sets fall back to TCP past 512 bytes of UDP spec (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes DNS for Services and Pods
StatefulSet start order ordinal, one at a time podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady default default (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes StatefulSet docs

Pitfalls

  • "A headless Service balances like a ClusterIP"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: same kind, same selector, and curl works.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: most HTTP clients take the first A record and stick to it, so one pod gets everything.
    ↳ Think instead: headless only helps a client that balances, such as gRPC round_robin or xDS.
  • Don't let clients resolve once and cache forever.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the default in many runtimes and connection pools.
    ↳ What goes wrong: scaled-up pods sit idle and replaced pods get connection errors.
    ↳ Do instead: re-resolve on a timer or on connection failure; set max_connection_age on servers.
  • Not the same: StatefulSet identity vs a stable IP
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the pod "keeps its name", so it feels like a fixed host.
    ↳ Difference: the DNS name and storage are stable; the IP behind them isn't.
    ↳ Think instead: address by name, every time.
  • "Not-ready pods are safe to publish"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: publishNotReadyAddresses fixes peer bootstrap.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: on a Service that clients also use, they now get pods that can't serve.
    ↳ Think instead: two Services: a headless one for peers, a normal one for clients.
  • Shelf life: DNS-returns-pods is durable; client libraries' re-resolution defaults move.

Connections

Path:Services and kube-proxyheadless ServicesCoreDNSinference LB
  • Builds on DNS-based service discovery: the same idea inside the cluster.
  • Owned elsewhere: gRPC load balancing owns client LB policies.
  • Breaks when combined with clients that resolve once at start-up.
  • Bounded by TTL and caching layers: change is seen only as fast as caches expire.

notes.title: Ingress vs Gateway API vs Service Mesh — North-South, East-West, and Who Owns Each Route
notes.html:
References

Gateway API: Introduction · Kubernetes: Ingress (frozen) · Kubernetes blog: Gateway API v1.6 · Kubernetes blog: Ingress NGINX retirement · Istio: Sidecar or ambient?

TL;DR

Three layers, two directions:

  • Ingress is the frozen 2020 API for traffic entering the cluster: host and path in the spec, everything else in vendor annotations.
  • Gateway API is its successor. Its roles are split: the platform owns the Gateway, app teams own HTTPRoutes. Headers, weights, gRPC, TLS and TCP routing are in the spec.
  • A service mesh handles east-west traffic between services: mTLS by workload identity, per-request balancing, retries and policy on calls that never touch the edge.

They compose. A gateway at the edge, a mesh inside, and Gateway API resources can configure both.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:clientcloud LBGateway (TLS, host and path match)HTTPRoute picks a Service, weightedpodeast-west call through the mesh (mTLS, per-request LB)next pod

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which direction does each handle? Ingress and Gateway: north-south. Mesh: east-west.
Why did Gateway API replace Ingress? Ingress standardised only host and path; the rest was unportable annotations.
The three Gateway API roles? GatewayClass (infra provider), Gateway (platform team), Route (app team).
What does a mesh add that a gateway can't? Identity-based mTLS and policy on service-to-service calls.
What happened to ingress-nginx? Retired: announced Nov 2025, best-effort maintenance ended Mar 2026.
Draw by hand: edge plus mesh internet → LB → Gateway box (platform-owned) → Routes (team-owned) → Services; inside, pod ↔ pod through mesh proxies with a lock icon; label the edge "north-south" and the inside "east-west".

The idea

A platform runs ingress-nginx with 400 Ingress objects. Canary weights, header matches, timeouts and CORS live in about 30 different annotations, half of them nginx-specific. Then ingress-nginx is retired. Moving to another controller means rewriting every annotation, because none of it was in the spec.

Gateway API puts that behaviour in typed fields, and splits ownership: the platform team owns one Gateway with the certificates and listeners, and each app team writes HTTPRoutes in its own namespace. The Gateway decides which namespaces may attach.

The trade: Gateway API and a mesh give portable, role-split routing at the edge and identity-aware policy inside, and you pay with more resource types, a controller (and maybe a mesh control plane) to run, and a migration off annotations.

How it works

Where each layer acts, and who owns it.

Rule What actually happens
No controller, no routing an Ingress or Gateway applies cleanly and does nothing until a controller implements it
Routes attach to Gateways parentRefs names the Gateway; the Gateway's allowedRoutes decides which namespaces may
Cross-namespace backends need consent a ReferenceGrant in the target namespace allows a Route to point at its Service
Gateways usually skip kube-proxy controllers read EndpointSlices and send to pod IPs, balancing per request
The mesh sits on every hop inside sidecars (per pod) or ambient ztunnel (per node) plus optional waypoint proxies for L7 
cross-AZ hops per east-west call, 3 AZs, zone-blind placement:
direct pod → pod                    1 hop × 2/3 = 0.67
hairpin pod → LB → ingress → pod    3 hops × 2/3 = 2.0     ← 3× the cross-AZ bytes

Evolution

Lineage:2017 Istio 0.1 sidecarsSep 2020 Ingress GA (1.19), then frozenOct 2023 Gateway API v1.0Nov 2024 Istio ambient GA (1.24)Nov 2025 ingress-nginx retirement announcedFeb 2026 v1.5 (ListenerSet, TLSRoute Standard)Jun 2026 v1.6 (TCPRoute, UDPRoute Standard)
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Nov 2026): core HTTP routing is GA; features graduate every release.
  • Changed recently: ingress-nginx stopped receiving fixes in Mar 2026; ambient meshes remove the per-pod sidecar; GAMMA lets Gateway API Routes configure mesh traffic.
  • What won't change: edge and inside are separate jobs, even when one product does both.

On the wire

One Gateway owned by the platform and one Route owned by a team, with the defaults that bite:

kind: Gateway                         # namespace: infra, owned by the platform team
metadata: { name: public, namespace: infra }
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy
  listeners:
  - name: https
    port: 443
    protocol: HTTPS
    tls: { certificateRefs: [{ name: wildcard-cert }] }
    allowedRoutes: { namespaces: { from: Selector, selector: { matchLabels: { edge: "true" } } } }
                                      # default from: Same — routes in team namespaces silently don't attach

kind: HTTPRoute                       # namespace: shop, owned by the app team
metadata: { name: orders, namespace: shop }
spec:
  parentRefs: [{ name: public, namespace: infra }]
  hostnames: ["shop.example.com"]
  rules:
  - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /orders } }]
    backendRefs:
    - { name: orders-v1, port: 80, weight: 90 }
    - { name: orders-v2, port: 80, weight: 10 }   # canary in the spec, not an annotation

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): east-west calls sent out to the ingress and back in ("hairpinning"), 3 AZs, zone-blind hops.

def crossings(hops, same_zone_last=False, trials=200_000):
    # walk `hops` steps, each to a random AZ (the last one stays local if same_zone_last)
    ...
print(crossings(1), crossings(1, True), crossings(3))
# look for: the hairpin row
# naive belief predicts: going through the ingress just adds a little latency

Run: 0.67 cross-AZ crossings per call direct, 0.0 with PreferSameZone, and 2.0 through the LB and an ingress pod. At 50 TB a day of east-west traffic that's about 100,000 GB crossing zone lines instead of 33,000, each billed on both sides, plus two extra proxy hops and an internet-facing path for internal calls.

Measure it

  • See it: kubectl get gateway,httproute -A and each Route's status.parents[].conditions (Accepted, ResolvedRefs): an unattached Route says why there.
  • In production: per-route request rate, p99 and 5xx from the gateway; mesh mTLS coverage (share of east-west requests with a peer identity); proxy memory per pod or node.
  • Bounded by: gateway config size ∝ total routes; mesh config ∝ services × proxies (why ambient exists); trust → mTLS.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Ingress is the frozen edge API: host and path, the rest annotations. Gateway API replaces it with typed routing and a role split: platform owns Gateways, teams own Routes. A mesh handles east-west traffic: workload-identity mTLS, per-request balancing, retries and policy between services. They compose: Gateway at the edge, mesh inside, and both can be configured with Gateway API resources.

Q · Mechanism — How does an HTTPRoute in namespace shop end up served by a Gateway in infra? The Route names the Gateway in parentRefs. The Gateway's listener allowedRoutes must admit the shop namespace; if it does, the controller marks the Route Accepted and compiles it into the proxy config. If the backend Service is in a third namespace, a ReferenceGrant there must allow it. Status conditions on the Route report each step.

Q · Trade-off — Sidecar mesh or ambient mesh? Sidecars give every pod a full L7 proxy: per-pod policy and telemetry, but memory and CPU per pod, config pushed to every proxy, and pod restarts to upgrade. Ambient puts L4 mTLS in a per-node ztunnel and adds L7 waypoints only where needed, cutting proxy count to roughly one per node. Ambient by default; sidecars where a workload needs per-pod L7 features.

Q · Failure — After moving to Gateway API, one team's routes return 404 while others work. Why? Their HTTPRoute isn't attached. The usual cause is the listener's allowedRoutes defaulting to Same namespace, or a hostname that doesn't match the listener's. kubectl describe httproute shows Accepted: False with a reason, while kubectl apply succeeded. Fix the selector, and alert on Routes whose Accepted condition is false.

Q · Design — Edge and service-to-service networking for a 40-team platform.

  • Edge: one shared Gateway per trust zone (public, partner) owned by the platform; teams attach HTTPRoutes from labelled namespaces.
  • Inside: ambient mesh for mTLS by default; waypoints for teams needing L7 retries or authz.
  • Internal calls: never through the public gateway; PreferSameZone on Services.
  • Migration: ingress-nginx annotations mapped to Route fields, one hostname at a time.
  • Watch first: unattached Routes, per-route 5xx and mTLS coverage.

Compare

Ingress Gateway API Service mesh
Direction north-south north-south (east-west via GAMMA) east-west
In the spec host, path, TLS host, path, headers, weights, gRPC, TLS, TCP, UDP mTLS, retries, LB, authz
Ownership model one object, one owner GatewayClass / Gateway / Route mesh-wide plus per-service policy
Status (Nov 2026) frozen v1.6, active Istio ambient GA, Linkerd, Cilium
Cost a controller a controller a control plane plus proxies

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Ingress routing fields in spec host and path the rest is annotations spec (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes Ingress
Gateway API roles 3 GatewayClass, Gateway, Route spec (as of Nov 2026): Gateway API introduction
Proxy hops per call, sidecar mesh 2 client and server sidecar default (as of Nov 2026): Istio data-plane modes
Cross-AZ crossings, hairpin vs direct 2.0 vs 0.67 3 AZs, zone-blind derived; model run 24 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Gateway or mesh: pick one"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: both are Envoy-shaped proxies with routing rules.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the gateway sees only traffic crossing the edge; most calls are east-west and never touch it.
    ↳ Think instead: edge and inside are two jobs; they compose.
  • Don't hairpin internal calls through the public ingress.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one URL works from everywhere, and the gateway already has auth.
    ↳ What goes wrong: three times the cross-AZ hops, two extra proxies, and internal APIs on an internet-facing path.
    ↳ Do instead: call the Service name, with mesh policy for auth.
  • "kubectl apply succeeded, so the route is live"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no error came back, and with Ingress an applied object usually did work.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: attachment is decided later by the controller; an unattached Route serves nothing.
    ↳ Think instead: read status.parents and alert on Accepted: False.
  • Not the same: API gateway vs Gateway API
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: one word apart.
    ↳ Difference: an API gateway is a product doing auth, quotas, API keys and developer portals; Gateway API is a Kubernetes routing spec that many products implement, some of them API gateways.
    ↳ Think instead: spec vs product (API gateway).
  • Don't stay on ingress-nginx.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it still runs, the manifests haven't changed, and migrating 400 Ingresses is real work.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it has had no security fixes since Mar 2026, on the one proxy every internet request touches.
    ↳ Do instead: move to a Gateway API implementation, route by route.
  • Shelf life: the edge-vs-inside split is durable; Gateway API channels, mesh modes and controller choices move each release.

Connections

Path:Servicesingress, gateway, meshnetwork policiesinference LB
  • Builds on L7 load balancing and service mesh.
  • Owned elsewhere: ingress controllers owns controller internals; mTLS owns workload identity.
  • Breaks when combined with internal calls routed through the public edge.
  • Bounded by the bill: every extra hop can cross a zone line.

notes.title: CoreDNS & In-Cluster Service Discovery — The Search List and ndots:5
notes.html:
References

Kubernetes: DNS for Services and Pods · Kubernetes: Debugging DNS resolution · Kubernetes: NodeLocal DNSCache · resolv.conf(5)

TL;DR

Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf points at CoreDNS and carries a search list (<ns>.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local, plus the node's domains) with ndots:5. That lets a pod call orders and get orders.shop.svc.cluster.local. The cost: any name with fewer than five dots, such as api.example.com, is tried against every search domain first. So one external lookup becomes 5 names × A and AAAA = 10 queries, and four of the five names fail. CoreDNS load and tail latency on external calls come from this.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:app resolves api.example.comfewer than 5 dots, so append each search domain4 NXDOMAINs from CoreDNSthen the name as typedanswerall of it twice, for A and AAAA

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why ndots:5? So svc.ns and pod.svc.ns-style names resolve through the search list first.
Queries for api.example.com from a pod? 10 with four search domains: 5 names, A and AAAA each.
The cheapest fix for external names? A trailing dot (api.example.com.), or ndots lowered via dnsConfig.

The idea

A service calls a payment provider at api.pay.example.com on every request. p99 latency has a 5-second spike a few times an hour, and the provider's own dashboard shows nothing. The pod's resolver asks CoreDNS for api.pay.example.com.shop.svc.cluster.local first, then three more wrong names, each A and AAAA, before trying the real name. When one of those ten UDP queries is dropped (conntrack races were a classic cause), glibc waits its 5-second timeout.

The trade: the search list makes short in-cluster names just work, and you pay with every external name being tried as an internal one first, multiplying DNS load and exposing calls to resolver timeouts.

How it works

Name the app asks for Dots ndots:5 behaviour Queries until answer
orders 0 search list first; first try hits 2
api.example.com 2 4 search misses, then absolute 10
api.example.com. absolute no search list 2
api.example.com with ndots:2 2 absolute first 2 
queries = (search domains tried + 1) × 2 record types   ← 4 misses + 1 hit = 5 names × 2 = 10

CoreDNS runs as a Deployment behind the kube-dns Service; its kubernetes plugin answers cluster names from EndpointSlices with a 30 s TTL, and forward sends the rest upstream. NodeLocal DNSCache adds a per-node cache that absorbs repeats.

Evolution

Lineage:2015 kube-dns (SkyDNS + dnsmasq)Dec 2018 CoreDNS the default (1.13)2020 NodeLocal DNSCache stable (1.18)2023 conntrack race fixes in kernels and kube-proxy
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: NodeLocal DNSCache and per-pod dnsConfig are routine; meshes such as Istio ambient can proxy DNS.
  • What won't change: ndots:5 remains the default because changing it would break existing short names.

On the wire

A pod's resolver config, and the per-pod override, with the default that bites:

kubectl exec app -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# search shop.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local ec2.internal
# nameserver 10.96.0.10
# options ndots:5        ← the default that bites: every external name tries 4 wrong names first

spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
    - { name: ndots, value: "2" }      # "svc.ns" still searched; "api.example.com" tried absolute first

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): how many names the resolver tries before an answer, with the search list above.

def tried(name, ndots, answers):
    rel = [f"{name}.{s}." for s in search]
    order = [name] if name.endswith(".") else ([name + "."] + rel if name.count(".") >= ndots else rel + [name + "."])
    return next(i for i, q in enumerate(order, 1) if q in answers)
# look for: api.example.com at ndots 5 vs 2
# naive belief predicts: one lookup per hostname

Run: api.example.com at ndots:5 tries 5 names (10 queries); with a trailing dot or ndots:2, 1 name (2 queries); orders hits on its first search domain either way.

Measure it

  • See it: kubectl exec app -- cat /etc/resolv.conf; CoreDNS with the log plugin shows the NXDOMAIN parade per lookup.
  • In production: CoreDNS coredns_dns_requests_total by rcode (NXDOMAIN share), coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds p99, and app DNS time in traces.
  • Bounded by: resolver timeouts → DNS as an outage cause; caching → TTL and caching layers.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Pods resolve through CoreDNS with a search list and ndots:5, which makes short Service names work. Any name with fewer than five dots is tried with each search domain first, so an external name costs about ten queries, most of them NXDOMAIN. Fix it with trailing dots or a lower ndots for pods that call outside, and NodeLocal DNSCache for load.

Q · Mechanism — Why ndots:5, and not 1? Kubernetes names have up to four dots in their short forms: svc, svc.ns, svc.ns.svc, and so on. With ndots:5, all of those go through the search list and resolve to the cluster name. With ndots:1, orders.shop would be tried as an internet name first. The default favours in-cluster names and taxes external ones.

Q · Trade-off — Lower ndots cluster-wide, or NodeLocal DNSCache? Lower ndots removes the wasted queries but can break apps that use partially qualified cluster names. NodeLocal DNSCache keeps behaviour identical and absorbs repeats on the node, but the queries still happen. Cache cluster-wide; lower ndots (or use trailing dots) per workload that calls external hosts heavily.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
ndots default in pods 5 kubelet-generated resolv.conf default (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes DNS for Pods
Queries for one external name 10 4 search domains, A + AAAA derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
glibc resolver timeout 5 s, 2 attempts why a dropped query is a 5 s spike default (as of Nov 2026): resolv.conf(5)
CoreDNS cluster-record TTL 30 s kubernetes plugin default (as of Nov 2026): CoreDNS docs

Pitfalls

  • "DNS is one query per hostname"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: dig on a laptop shows one query and one answer.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the pod's resolver walks the search list first, so an external name is ten queries, eight of them NXDOMAIN.
    ↳ Think instead: count names tried × record types.
  • Don't set ndots:1 cluster-wide.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it removes the wasted queries in one change.
    ↳ What goes wrong: names like orders.shop go to the internet first and fail or resolve to someone else.
    ↳ Do instead: per-workload dnsConfig, or trailing dots in config.
  • Not the same: CoreDNS TTL vs client caching
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both decide how stale an answer is.
    ↳ Difference: the TTL is what CoreDNS sends; JVMs, Go and pools cache by their own rules, sometimes forever.
    ↳ Think instead: check the client's cache settings as well.
  • "5-second spikes are the remote API"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the slow call is the remote one.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a dropped UDP DNS query costs exactly the resolver's 5 s timeout before the call even starts.
    ↳ Think instead: time DNS separately in traces; a spike of exactly 5 s points at resolution.
  • Shelf life: search-list mechanics are durable; resolver defaults and DNS proxying in meshes move.

Connections

Path:headless ServicesCoreDNSnetwork policies (which must allow port 53)
  • Builds on DNS resolution: stub resolvers and recursion.
  • Owned elsewhere: TTL and caching layers owns cache behaviour.
  • Breaks when combined with a default-deny egress policy that forgets UDP and TCP 53 to kube-dns.
  • Bounded by DNS as an outage cause.

notes.title: Network Policies — Allow-Only Rules That Isolate a Pod the Moment One Selects It
notes.html:
References

Kubernetes: Network Policies · Network Policy API: AdminNetworkPolicy · Cilium: Network policy · AWS EKS: Network policies

TL;DR

With no policies, every pod reaches every pod. A NetworkPolicy flips one pod into isolated for a direction (ingress, egress or both) the moment any policy selects it; from then on only what some policy allows gets through. There are no deny rules: the effective rule is the union of every policy selecting the pod. The API stores policies whether or not anything enforces them, so on a CNI without enforcement they're silent no-ops.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:default-deny selects every pod in the namespaceall ingress and egress droppedadd allow: frontend → orders on 8080add allow: egress to kube-dns on 53everything else stays dropped

Recall

Prompt Answer
What happens when one policy selects a pod? That pod is isolated for the listed directions; only allowed traffic passes.
How do two policies on one pod combine? Union of allows; order never matters; no denies.
The first thing a default-deny egress breaks? DNS: allow UDP and TCP 53 to kube-dns.

The idea

A team adds a default-deny egress policy to a namespace on Friday. Every service in it starts failing with "unknown host". The policy was correct, but name resolution is egress too: pods could no longer reach CoreDNS on port 53. Nothing in the policy mentioned DNS, so nothing allowed it.

The trade: allow-only policies make isolation additive and order-free, and you pay by having to list every dependency, DNS included, with no deny rule to carve exceptions and no error when the CNI ignores it all.

How it works

Rule What actually happens
Selection isolates a pod selected by any policy with Ingress in policyTypes drops all ingress not allowed by some policy
Allow-only, unioned every allowing rule from every selecting policy adds up; there's no precedence
Peers by label or CIDR podSelector, namespaceSelector (both in one item = AND, separate items = OR), ipBlock
Stateful replies to an allowed connection are allowed; you don't write return rules
Enforced by the CNI Calico, Cilium, VPC CNI with its policy agent; Flannel ignores policies
Cluster-wide guardrails AdminNetworkPolicy (v1alpha1) adds admin-tier deny and pass rules above namespace policies

Evolution

Lineage:2016 NetworkPolicy beta (1.3)Jun 2017 GA (1.7)2018 egress rules (1.12)2023 AdminNetworkPolicy alphaAug 2023 VPC CNI enforcement
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026) for NetworkPolicy; AdminNetworkPolicy still alpha.
  • Changed recently: CNIs add L7 and FQDN rules (Cilium toFQDNs) outside the core API.
  • What won't change: core NetworkPolicy is L3/L4 and allow-only.

On the wire

Default-deny plus the two allows every namespace needs, with the defaults that bite:

kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector: {}                   # every pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]    # omit Egress and egress stays wide open

kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: allow-dns, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } },
           podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } } }]   # one item: namespace AND pod
    ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }]  # TCP too: big answers

Measure it

  • See it: after each policy change, kubectl exec a test pod and nc -zv an allowed and a denied target: one must connect, one must time out.
  • In production: policy drops from the CNI (Cilium Hubble policy-verdict, Calico flow logs, VPC CNI policy agent logs), and pods with no selecting policy.
  • Bounded by: CNI enforcement → CNI plugins; hostname egress → security posture.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The cluster is open by default. A NetworkPolicy isolates any pod it selects for the listed directions, and from then on only allowed traffic passes. Rules are allow-only and unioned, so there's no order. Start each namespace with default-deny for both directions plus DNS, then add allows per dependency, and test that the CNI actually enforces it.

Q · Mechanism — What's the difference between one from item with both selectors and two items? One item with namespaceSelector and podSelector means pods matching the label in namespaces matching the label: AND. Two separate items mean any pod in those namespaces, or matching pods in the policy's own namespace: OR. A misplaced dash turns a narrow rule into a wide one, and nothing warns you.

Q · Trade-off — Namespace NetworkPolicies or CNI-specific policy (Cilium, Calico)? Core NetworkPolicy is portable but L3/L4 only, allow-only and namespace-scoped. CNI policies add deny rules, cluster-wide scope, L7 matching and FQDN egress, but tie you to that CNI. Core policy for team-owned rules; CNI or AdminNetworkPolicy for platform guardrails teams can't override.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Default reachability all pods ↔ all pods no policies spec (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes network model
Rule kinds in core API allow only union of all selecting policies spec (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes Network Policies
DNS ports to allow UDP and TCP 53 TCP for large answers spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 7766

Pitfalls

  • "Policies applied, so traffic is blocked"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: kubectl apply succeeded and the object exists.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the API server stores them either way; a CNI that doesn't enforce ignores them, with no event or error.
    ↳ Think instead: a denied nc is the only proof, after every change.
  • Don't deploy default-deny egress without DNS.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the policy looks complete for the app's real dependencies.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every name lookup fails, so everything looks like an outage of everything.
    ↳ Do instead: ship allow-dns in the same change, UDP and TCP.
  • Not the same: AND vs OR in from
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the YAML differs by a single leading dash.
    ↳ Difference: one item with two selectors is AND; two items is OR, which is far wider.
    ↳ Think instead: read each list item as one peer, and test both sides.
  • "NetworkPolicy can allow api.stripe.com"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: egress allow-lists are usually written as hostnames.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: core policy matches pod labels, namespaces and IP blocks only, and SaaS and CDN addresses are shared and rotate.
    ↳ Think instead: FQDN rules in the CNI or an egress proxy (posture).
  • Shelf life: allow-only and selection-isolates are durable; AdminNetworkPolicy and CNI extensions move.

Connections

Path:flat networknetwork policiesprobes (kubelet probes come from the node, so allow them)
  • Builds on security groups vs NACLs: stateful allow rules, one layer down.
  • Owned elsewhere: CNI plugins own enforcement; mTLS owns identity-based authz.
  • Breaks when combined with a CNI without enforcement.
  • Bounded by label hygiene: a policy is only as good as the labels it selects.

notes.title: Probes vs Load Balancer Health Checks — Two Systems, Two Consequences
notes.html:
References

Kubernetes: Liveness, readiness and startup probes · Kubernetes: Configure probes · AWS Load Balancer Controller: target health

TL;DR

Three kubelet probes, three consequences:

  • Liveness failure restarts the container.
  • Readiness failure removes the pod from endpoints; it keeps running.
  • Startup holds the other two off until it passes.

Separately, a cloud load balancer runs its own health checks against nodes or pod IPs and keeps its own target list. The two systems don't wait for each other, so a pod can be Ready while the LB still marks it unhealthy, or the reverse. A pod readiness gate joins them.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:pod startsstartup probe passesreadiness passes, pod enters EndpointSlicesLB health check passes, target healthytrafficdependency blipsreadiness fails, pod drainedliveness untouched, no restart

Recall

Prompt Answer
Liveness vs readiness, by consequence? Liveness restarts; readiness only removes from endpoints.
What's a startup probe for? Slow starts: liveness and readiness don't run until it passes.
The dangerous probe mistake? Liveness checking a shared dependency: one blip restarts the fleet.

The idea

A service's liveness probe calls /health, which checks the database. The database fails over, taking 20 seconds. Every pod's liveness fails three times and every pod restarts at once. When the database is back, the fleet is cold-starting, connection pools are empty, and the restart storm hits the database again.

The pods were fine. The probe asked "can I reach my dependency?", which is a readiness question, and gave it a liveness consequence.

The trade: probes let Kubernetes heal and route around bad pods automatically, and you pay when the question a probe asks doesn't match its consequence: a restart for a dependency blip, or traffic to a pod still warming.

How it works

Budget for one pod: how long each failure takes to act, from the probe settings.

Probe Settings Time to act Consequence
startup periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 30 up to 300 s allowed to start restart if never passes
readiness periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 2 ≈ 10 s removed from endpoints
liveness periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3 ≈ 30 s container restarted
ALB target check interval 15 s, unhealthy threshold 2 ≈ 30 s LB stops sending 
time to act ≈ periodSeconds × failureThreshold       ← 5 × 2 = 10 s readiness; 10 × 3 = 30 s liveness
startup window = periodSeconds × failureThreshold   ← 10 × 30 = 300 s for a model load

kubectl get pod app-7f9 -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'   # Ready, ContainersReady, and any readiness gate
kubectl describe pod app-7f9 | grep -A3 -i probe              # failures and their reasons

Evolution

Lineage:2015 liveness and readiness probes2019 pod readiness gatesDec 2020 startup probes GA (1.20)Apr 2023 gRPC probes GA (1.27)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: gRPC probes are native; AWS and GKE controllers inject readiness gates so a pod isn't Ready until the LB sees it healthy.
  • What won't change: two independent health systems, each with its own clock.

On the wire

Probes for a model server that takes minutes to load, with the defaults that bite:

containers:
- name: server
  startupProbe:   { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 30 }
  readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5,  failureThreshold: 2 }
                  # /ready may check dependencies and warm-up: failing only drains traffic
  livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /live,  port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3 }
                  # /live checks THIS process only. Default timeoutSeconds is 1 s:
                  # a GC pause or busy event loop past 1 s counts as a failure

Measure it

  • See it: kubectl describe pod lists probe failures; restart count (kubectl get pods) shows liveness kills.
  • In production: container restarts per hour by reason; pods NotReady; LB unhealthy target count next to the Service's ready endpoint count (they should match).
  • Bounded by: drain on shutdown → rollouts; LB-side checks → health checks.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Liveness restarts, readiness drains, startup protects slow starts. Liveness must check only the process itself; readiness can check dependencies and warm-up. The cloud LB runs its own health checks on its own schedule, so I use a readiness gate to keep the two in step, and I size thresholds so a probe acts in seconds, not minutes.

Q · Mechanism — Why can a pod be Ready but get no traffic from the LB? The LB's target group has its own health checks and thresholds. A new pod enters EndpointSlices when its readiness passes, the controller registers it, and the LB marks it healthy only after its own checks pass, often 30 s later. Without a readiness gate, a rollout can kill old pods before the new ones are healthy at the LB.

Q · Trade-off — Aggressive or relaxed probe thresholds? Aggressive readiness drains a sick pod in seconds but can flap under load spikes. Aggressive liveness restarts hung pods quickly but turns a GC pause or a slow dependency into a restart storm. Fast readiness, slow and process-only liveness.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Probe defaults period 10 s, timeout 1 s, failure threshold 3 apply when unset default (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes configure probes
Liveness time to act 30 s 10 s × 3 derived from the defaults
Startup window in the example 300 s 10 s × 30 derived from the config above

Pitfalls

  • "Liveness should check the database"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "healthy" feels like "can do its job".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a shared dependency blip fails every pod's liveness at once and restarts the fleet.
    ↳ Think instead: liveness = this process is wedged; dependencies belong in readiness.
  • Don't use liveness to cover a slow start.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a long initialDelaySeconds seems to work.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a slower start (a bigger model, a cold cache) gets killed in a loop.
    ↳ Do instead: a startup probe sized for the worst start.
  • Not the same: Ready in Kubernetes vs healthy at the LB
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both decide whether a pod gets traffic.
    ↳ Difference: readiness gates the EndpointSlice; the LB gates its own target list, on its own clock.
    ↳ Think instead: join them with a readiness gate.
  • "A 1-second timeout is plenty for /live"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the endpoint returns in milliseconds on a laptop.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: under load a GC pause or saturated worker pool passes 1 s, and three misses restart a pod that was only busy.
    ↳ Think instead: set timeoutSeconds from p99.9 under load.
  • Shelf life: the three consequences are durable; controller readiness-gate behaviour moves.

Connections

Path:Servicesprobes vs LB checksrollouts
  • Builds on health checks: active checks at the LB.
  • Owned elsewhere: outlier detection owns passive health.
  • Breaks when combined with liveness probes that call shared dependencies.
  • Bounded by cascading failures: restart storms are one.

notes.title: Rollouts & Connection Handling — The Race Between SIGTERM and Endpoint Removal
notes.html:
References

Kubernetes: Pod termination · Kubernetes: Container lifecycle hooks · Kubernetes: EndpointSlice conditions · AWS Load Balancer Controller: deregistration delay

TL;DR

When a pod is deleted, two things start at the same time:

  • the kubelet sends SIGTERM, via preStop if one is set;
  • the control plane removes the pod from EndpointSlices, then every node's kube-proxy, every gateway and the cloud LB catch up, each with its own lag.

If the app stops accepting before the last of them has caught up, callers get refused connections. The fix is to keep serving while the world forgets you: a preStop sleep longer than the propagation lag, then a graceful drain, all inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:pod deleted(endpoint removal ‖ preStop sleep 10 s)nodes and LB stop routing hereSIGTERMstop accepting, finish in-flightexitSIGKILL only if the grace period ends first

Recall

Prompt Answer
What happens at pod deletion, in what order? Endpoint removal and preStop/SIGTERM start together; no ordering.
What is preStop sleep for? Keep serving while removal reaches every node and LB.
What cuts a drain short? terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 s) expiring → SIGKILL.

The idea

Every deploy of a checkout service shows a burst of 502s and connection resets for a few seconds. The app handles SIGTERM correctly: it stops accepting and finishes in-flight requests. That's the problem. Remote nodes still have the pod in their rules for a second or two, and the ALB for longer, so new connections keep arriving at a process that has stopped listening.

The trade: decoupled termination lets Kubernetes tear pods down without a global lock, and you pay by having to outlast the slowest component's lag yourself, with sleeps and grace periods that slow every rollout.

How it works

The termination budget, with every term derived:

Phase Duration Why
preStop: sleep 10 s outlast node rule sync and LB deregistration start
drain in-flight after SIGTERM up to 25 s p99.9 request (or one streamed response)
margin 5 s flush logs and close pools
terminationGracePeriodSeconds 40 s 10 + 25 + 5; the preStop time counts against it 
grace ≥ preStop sleep + longest in-flight work + margin     ← 10 + 25 + 5 = 40 s
default grace 30 s < 40 s   → SIGKILL mid-drain on the slowest requests
long-lived streams: the drain must outlast the CONNECTION, or the server must send GOAWAY / close and let clients reconnect

kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=checkout -o yaml | grep -B2 -A3 terminating
# conditions: { ready: false, serving: true, terminating: true }   ← still finishing, no new traffic

Run (model, Python 3.15, 24 Nov 2026): per-caller propagation lag drawn lognormal with a 1 s median; the app stops accepting after the preStop sleep. Requests refused in the first 10 s: 11.91 % with no sleep, 1.00 % with 2 s, 0.04 % with 5 s, 0.00 % with 10 s. The naive belief, "handling SIGTERM gracefully is enough", predicts zero for the first row.

Evolution

Lineage:2015 preStop hooks and grace periods2020 EndpointSlices2022 serving and terminating endpoint conditionsApr 2025 native sidecars stable (1.33)Aug 2025 sleep action for preStop GA (1.34)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: a built-in preStop: sleep needs no shell in the image; native sidecars stop after the app, so mesh proxies no longer die first.
  • What won't change: removal and SIGTERM are concurrent by design.

On the wire

A pod spec that drains cleanly, with the defaults that bite:

spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40     # default 30: SIGKILL arrives mid-drain for slow requests
  containers:
  - name: app
    lifecycle:
      preStop: { sleep: { seconds: 10 } }   # no default: without it the app stops accepting at once
    # app on SIGTERM: stop accepting, finish in-flight, close keep-alive conns with Connection: close
# Deployment: maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 25%   ← default 25% unavailable drops capacity mid-rollout

Measure it

  • See it: a load generator during a rollout (hey or k6 at steady RPS) counting 5xx and resets per second; kubectl get events for Killing with exit 137 (SIGKILL).
  • In production: 5xx and resets per deploy window, containers ending with exit code 137, and LB TargetDeregistration timings.
  • Bounded by: LB deregistration delay → health checks; long connections → long-lived connections.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: At pod deletion, endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen concurrently, and every node and LB learns about removal with some lag. If the app stops accepting first, callers get refused. So: a preStop sleep longer than that lag, then stop accepting and drain, with a grace period that covers sleep plus the longest request. Plus maxUnavailable: 0 so capacity never drops.

Q · Mechanism — Why doesn't Kubernetes just remove the endpoint first and then send SIGTERM? There's no global barrier: kube-proxy on hundreds of nodes, gateways and cloud LBs each watch and apply changes on their own schedule, and none of them reports back "done". The kubelet can't know when the last one caught up, so it starts termination at once and leaves the waiting to you.

Q · Trade-off — Long grace periods or fast rollouts? A long preStop and grace period make deploys clean but slow, and a node drain waits for every pod on it. Short ones roll fast and drop requests. Size the sleep to measured propagation lag, the drain to p99.9 request time, and handle long-lived streams by closing them gracefully so clients reconnect elsewhere.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Default grace period 30 s preStop time counts against it default (as of Nov 2026): Kubernetes pod lifecycle
Refused requests, no preStop sleep 11.91 % of the first 10 s 1 s median lag model derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Refused requests, 10 s sleep 0.00 % same model derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
ALB deregistration delay 300 s target-group default default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ELB docs

Pitfalls

  • "Handling SIGTERM gracefully means zero-downtime deploys"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the app finishes every request it has.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: new connections keep arriving after SIGTERM, until every node and LB has forgotten the pod.
    ↳ Think instead: keep accepting through a preStop sleep, then drain.
  • Don't leave the grace period at 30 s with a long preStop.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the sleep and the drain each look short on their own.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the sleep eats the budget and SIGKILL lands mid-request (exit 137).
    ↳ Do instead: grace = sleep + longest in-flight work + margin.
  • Not the same: ready: false vs serving: false
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both mean "don't send new traffic" in casual talk.
    ↳ Difference: a terminating pod is not ready but can still be serving; gateways may use it as a last resort.
    ↳ Think instead: read all three endpoint conditions.
  • "WebSocket and gRPC streams drain like requests"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the same SIGTERM handler covers both.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a stream can outlive any grace period; it ends in SIGKILL and a client error.
    ↳ Think instead: send GOAWAY or a close frame, and let clients reconnect.
  • Shelf life: the race is durable; preStop actions and endpoint conditions keep improving.

Connections

Path:probesrollouts and connection handlinginference LB
  • Builds on connection teardown and Services.
  • Owned elsewhere: long-lived connections owns stream draining at scale.
  • Breaks when combined with a default grace period and a long sleep.
  • Bounded by the slowest component's propagation lag, usually the cloud LB.

notes.title: Load Balancing GPU & Inference Workloads — Count Work, Not Turns
notes.html:
References

Gateway API Inference Extension · Kubernetes blog: Introducing Gateway API Inference Extension · Envoy: Load balancers (least request, P2C) · Mitzenmacher: The power of two choices

TL;DR
