An inference request can cost 200 ms or 60 s depending on the prompt and output length. So round robin counts turns, not work: it keeps feeding a pod stuck on long generations while others idle.

  • The minimum: least request (fewest in flight), or power of two choices over in-flight counts.
  • Better: route on the server's own signals, its queue depth and KV-cache use, and prefer a pod that already caches this prompt's prefix.

The Gateway API Inference Extension standardises this: an InferencePool of model-server pods with an endpoint picker in front.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:requestGatewayHTTPRoute to an InferencePoolendpoint picker reads queue depth, KV-cache use, prefix matchchooses a podstreams tokens back

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why is round robin wrong for inference? Request cost varies 100×; turns ≠ work.
What signal beats in-flight count? The server's queue depth and KV-cache use, plus prefix-cache affinity.
What does a ClusterIP do here? Pins each connection to one pod; no algorithm downstream can fix it.

The idea

Eight GPU pods serve a chat model behind a round-robin gateway. Most requests are short, but one in five asks for a long generation. Round robin hands a pod its next request on schedule whether it's free or three long generations deep. Median latency is tens of seconds at 85 % utilisation, and the cluster autoscaler is asked for more GPUs while some pods sit idle.

The trade: load-aware routing turns the same GPUs into much lower latency, and you pay with a router that must read live server state (an extra component, and a failure mode if its signals go stale).

How it works

Algorithm Signal What it misses
round robin none request cost; a slow pod keeps getting its turn
least request in-flight count at the proxy a pod's real queue and memory pressure
power of two choices in-flight count of 2 random pods same, but cheap and herd-proof across many proxies
endpoint picker (InferencePool) queue depth, KV-cache use, LoRA adapters loaded, prefix match needs model-server metrics; picker is a dependency

Run (model, Python 3.15, 24 Nov 2026): 8 pods, 85 % utilisation, 80 % of requests 0.2 s and 20 % 6 s, one sequence per pod (a simplification; real servers batch). Latency including queueing:

Policy p50 p99
round robin 9.53 s 61.23 s
power of two choices 5.49 s 24.81 s
least request 0.33 s 17.98 s

The naive belief, "with enough pods every policy averages out", predicts three equal rows. Same pods, same load: only the choice changed.

Evolution

Lineage:1996 power of two choices2017 Envoy least request with P2C2023 continuous batching and paged KV cache (vLLM)Jun 2025 Gateway API Inference Extension announced2025 InferencePool v1 GA; InferenceModel replaced by InferenceObjective
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Nov 2026): InferencePool is v1; objectives and picker plugins still change.
  • Changed recently: prefix-cache-aware routing and disaggregated prefill/decode pools (llm-d, vLLM, SGLang).
  • What won't change: balance on work, and per request, never per connection.

On the wire

An InferencePool behind a Gateway route, with the defaults that bite:

apiVersion: inference.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: InferencePool
metadata: { name: chat-pool, namespace: ml }
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: vllm-chat } }
  targetPorts: [{ number: 8000 }]
  endpointPickerRef: { name: chat-epp, port: { number: 9002 } }   # the picker reads server metrics

kind: HTTPRoute
spec:
  parentRefs: [{ name: inference-gw }]
  rules:
  - backendRefs: [{ group: inference.networking.k8s.io, kind: InferencePool, name: chat-pool }]
# the default that bites: pointing the route at a plain Service instead gives the gateway's
# default policy (often round robin) and no queue or cache signals at all

Measure it

  • See it: per-pod in-flight requests and queue depth from the model server (vllm:num_requests_waiting, KV-cache usage) side by side.
  • In production: max-to-median in-flight per pod (the imbalance detector), time to first token p99, GPU utilisation spread across pods, prefix-cache hit rate.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Inference requests vary 100× in cost, so round robin piles work on busy pods. At minimum use least request or power of two choices per request, never a ClusterIP that pins connections. Better is a picker that reads each server's queue depth and KV-cache use and prefers pods with the prompt's prefix cached: that's what the Gateway API InferencePool standardises.

Q · Mechanism — Why does power of two choices beat plain least request across many gateway replicas? Each gateway replica has only its own in-flight counts. If all of them send to the global least-loaded pod, they herd onto it together. Picking the better of two random pods spreads choices while still avoiding the worst ones, and its maximum load is exponentially better than random.

Q · Trade-off — Prefix-cache affinity or pure load balance? Affinity sends requests sharing a system prompt to the pod that already holds its KV cache, cutting prefill time. Pushed too far, it concentrates load on hot pods. Pickers score both: prefer the cached pod unless its queue is past a threshold.

Pitfalls

  • "Round robin is fair, so it's fine"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every pod gets the same number of requests, and it's the default in most gateways.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the same count isn't the same work when requests vary 100× in cost.
    ↳ Think instead: balance in-flight work, or the server's own queue.
  • Don't put an inference fleet behind a ClusterIP.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the default Service, and it works in a demo.
    ↳ What goes wrong: HTTP/2 connections pin, so a few pods take everything while GPUs idle.
    ↳ Do instead: InferencePool, or a headless Service with per-request LB.
  • Not the same: GPU utilisation vs pod load
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: busy GPUs look like a busy fleet.
    ↳ Difference: average utilisation can be fine while some pods queue for seconds and others idle.
    ↳ Think instead: watch max-to-median per pod, not the fleet average.
  • "Autoscale on GPU utilisation"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the scarce, expensive resource, and every dashboard shows it first.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: batching servers run near full utilisation at any load; queue depth is what rises first.
    ↳ Think instead: scale on queue depth or waiting requests.
  • Shelf life: count-work-not-turns is durable; InferencePool fields and picker plugins move fast.
